Newborn Care

White spots on the nipple: milk blebs and other causes

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A pale dot on a nipple can be uncomfortable and worrying. The right response depends on its cause. Avoid picking or draining it, and get help when pain, feeding problems or other breast changes are present.

A white spot is a finding, not a diagnosis

A small pale spot on the nipple during breastfeeding may be a milk bleb, but its colour alone cannot establish the cause. A blister from friction, an irritated area of skin, a normal gland on the areola or an infection can look different in person from a photograph. A spot outside breastfeeding also deserves assessment if it is new, painful or persistent.

Notice whether there is one fixed dot or several blisters, whether the nipple changes colour after a feed, and whether the surrounding skin is sore, scaly or swollen. Mention any breast lump, discharge, fever or feeding difficulty. These details help a clinician distinguish causes that need different treatment.

Milk blebs and inflammation at the nipple opening

Milk leaves the breast through small openings in the nipple. A bleb can look like a tiny white, yellowish or pink dot and may cause sharp or stinging pain during feeding. The surrounding area may also feel irritated. Some people have one episode; others experience recurrent spots or other breast inflammation.

A bleb is better understood as an inflammatory problem at a duct opening than as a solid lump of milk that must be squeezed out. It can occur alongside narrowed, inflamed ducts or oversupply. It does not automatically mean there is a bacterial infection or that antibiotics are required.

Ask a breastfeeding medicine clinician or other qualified professional to assess a suspected bleb, particularly if feeding hurts. They can review both the visible spot and contributing problems. A baby sucking harder is not a treatment you need to force.

Treat the cause without opening or scraping the spot

Do not pierce a suspected bleb with a needle, pick off its surface or scrub it with a cloth. Opening the skin can worsen trauma and narrowing. Strong squeezing and deep breast massage can also injure inflamed tissue. Searching for a home drainage technique is not a substitute for assessment.

A clinician may prescribe a topical anti-inflammatory treatment, such as a suitable steroid cream, and explain how to use it around feeds. Some clinicians consider lecithin as part of an individual plan. Neither is a reason to start a medicine or supplement without checking the diagnosis and instructions.

A cool compress and an appropriate pain reliever may help discomfort when suitable for you. Heat is not required to “melt” a blockage and can worsen swelling, although brief warmth may feel comforting to some people. Avoid prolonged soaking or anything that leaves the nipple more irritated. If the plan is not helping, arrange reassessment rather than repeatedly trying more force.

Feeding and expressing: avoid chasing an empty breast

Breasts continue making milk; they do not need to be completely emptied at each feed. Continue responsive feeding as comfortable and seek help with positioning and attachment. A nipple that looks flattened or white after feeding can reflect compression and needs a feeding assessment rather than treatment as a fixed milk bleb.

Adding repeated feeds or pumping sessions solely to clear a spot can increase milk production and worsen an oversupply cycle. There is no universal instruction to begin every feed on the affected side. If you are expressing while separated from your baby, aim for the amount normally needed rather than repeatedly pumping to empty.

If pain or swelling prevents feeding or expressing, get prompt help with a workable plan for your comfort and the baby’s intake. Check pump fit and suction with a knowledgeable professional. Do not simply wait several weeks for painful feeding to resolve, and do not blame yourself for having offered the other breast.

Pressure and normal pregnancy-related bumps

Clothing or equipment that presses uncomfortably on the breast can add irritation. Choose a supportive bra that fits, adjust a carrier as instructed and avoid prolonged local pressure. An underwire is not automatically a problem if the bra fits properly. Continue using a correctly positioned seat belt; the answer to discomfort is safe adjustment, not travelling without restraint.

During pregnancy and breastfeeding, small bumps on the darker skin around the nipple may become more visible. These are often Montgomery glands, which produce protective oils. Their normal appearance and number vary, and they may remain noticeable after breastfeeding ends.

Normal areolar glands do not need to be popped, scrubbed or removed. If a bump becomes painful, markedly swollen or inflamed, or you are unsure that it is a normal gland, have it checked. Pregnancy does not make every new nipple change harmless.

When thrush is considered: and why an examination matters

Candida can cause oral thrush in a baby and can be considered when assessing irritated nipple skin. Recent antibiotic use or a history of fungal infection may be relevant. Possible symptoms include burning soreness, itching, shiny or flaky skin and white patches, but these overlap with problems such as poor attachment or dermatitis.

A baby with oral thrush may have creamy patches inside the cheeks, on the gums or on the tongue that do not wipe away easily, and may be unsettled when feeding. Milk residue alone is not proof of thrush. Tell the clinician about symptoms in both you and the baby rather than treating a white dot as a confirmed infection.

If thrush is diagnosed, the clinician may recommend an antifungal preparation for the parent and an age-appropriate treatment for the baby when needed. Follow the exact instructions; do not share adult creams or oral medicines with an infant. Handwashing, clean feeding equipment and regularly changed breast pads are sensible parts of care.

The explanation sometimes called “deep breast thrush” is debated and should not be used to explain persistent breast pain automatically. If antifungal treatment does not help, the diagnosis needs another look. This uncertainty does not dismiss your pain; it helps avoid repeatedly treating the wrong cause.

Blisters that could be herpes need prompt medical advice

Herpes simplex can occasionally affect the breast, producing painful grouped fluid-filled blisters or sores that later crust. They may be mistaken for another skin condition. Arrange prompt assessment if herpes is possible; a clinician may test the lesions and prescribe antiviral treatment. Do not assume every case needs the same fixed treatment duration.

With active herpes lesions on a breast, do not breastfeed or give expressed milk from that side until the lesions have healed and the clinician says feeding can resume. Milk expressed from the affected side during this period should be discarded. Expressing may help maintain production while a feeding plan is arranged.

Feeding from an unaffected breast may be possible if the affected lesions are fully covered and careful hand and pump hygiene is followed. Get urgent paediatric advice after possible infant exposure, especially if the baby develops blisters or becomes unwell. Herpes in a young baby can be serious, so this situation should not be managed as an ordinary milk bleb.

Persistent nipple changes and the uncommon cancer question

Most nipple spots have a non-cancerous explanation. Nevertheless, a persistent scaly, itchy, sore or crusted nipple rash, new flattening or inward pulling, unusual yellow or bloody discharge, or a breast lump needs medical examination. This applies whether or not you are breastfeeding.

One uncommon cause is Paget’s disease of the nipple, which is associated with breast cancer and can resemble eczema. A small skin biopsy may be needed to confirm it, with breast imaging to assess associated disease. Treatment commonly involves surgery, but its extent and any additional treatment depend on the findings; it is not simply a matter of removing a visible white patch.

Do not interpret the percentage of breast cancers associated with Paget’s disease as the chance that your spot is cancer. Equally, do not keep extending home treatment for a persistent nipple change. Ask for an examination and a follow-up plan if the first treatment does not resolve it.

Deciding how quickly to seek care

Contact a healthcare professional promptly for a painful or persistent spot, feeding that is difficult because of pain, a new lump, abnormal discharge, or a new change in nipple shape or skin. Severe pain is a reason to ask for help now, not after an arbitrary week of home treatment.

Fever, chills, spreading breast inflammation or feeling systemically unwell need timely assessment. Seek urgent care if you are rapidly worsening or very unwell. Possible herpes exposure in a young baby needs prompt medical advice even when the parent’s own lesion seems small.

Bring a list of creams, supplements and feeding changes you have tried. If appearance changes between feeds, a private photograph may help show the clinician what you mean. The aim is a clear diagnosis and comfortable, sustainable feeding: not enduring pain until the spot eventually disappears.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current breastfeeding guidance advises against opening milk blebs or aggressive massage.

Persistent nipple pain needs assessment; appearance alone does not establish thrush.

Active herpes on a breast requires specific feeding precautions until the lesions heal.

How BeMama can help

Use the symptom pattern, feeding history and questions in this guide to prepare for an examination by a clinician or breastfeeding specialist.

When to seek help

Fever with worsening breast symptoms, severe illness, suspected breast herpes or a persistent nipple rash/lump needs medical attention. Never pierce a bleb or feed milk from a breast with active herpes lesions.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A milk bleb is not something to squeeze or open.
  • Extra pumping to empty can worsen oversupply and inflammation.
  • Normal Montgomery glands are different from a painful nipple lesion.
  • Persistent rash, abnormal discharge or a new lump should be examined.

Frequently asked questions

Can I open a milk bleb with a sterilised needle?

No. Puncturing or removing its surface can worsen injury. Have the spot assessed and use the recommended treatment for its cause rather than trying to release a plug.

Should I pump more until the breast is empty?

Avoid adding pumping solely to clear the spot. Extra removal can drive oversupply. Ask for an individual plan if ordinary feeding or expressing is painful or difficult.

Does a bleb mean I need antibiotics?

Not automatically. Blebs involve inflammation, and antibiotics are used when a clinician identifies an appropriate bacterial indication. Fever or worsening breast symptoms need assessment.

Are the little bumps around my nipple during pregnancy normal?

They may be Montgomery glands, which help protect the nipple and areola. They do not need squeezing. A painful, inflamed, changing or unfamiliar bump should be checked.

Does a white spot prove that I have thrush?

No. Skin irritation, a bleb and other causes can look pale. An examination and review of symptoms in parent and baby help determine whether an antifungal treatment is appropriate.

Can I keep feeding with suspected herpes on the breast?

Get prompt medical advice and avoid feeding from a breast with active herpes lesions. Follow the clinician’s plan for the affected milk, the unaffected side and resuming feeding after healing.

Does a white nipple after feeding mean a blocked pore?

Not necessarily. A nipple that becomes flattened or white after a feed may be compressed. Have positioning, attachment and the pattern of pain checked rather than treating it as a fixed spot.

Could a persistent nipple rash be cancer?

Most changes are not cancer, but a persistent nipple rash needs examination. Paget’s disease is an uncommon possibility, and a biopsy may be needed if it is suspected. A new lump or unusual discharge should also be checked.

How long should I wait if feeding is very painful?

Ask for help promptly. You do not need to wait a week or several weeks with severe pain. Fever, worsening inflammation, significant illness or concern about infant exposure to herpes needs more urgent advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
